c.tagline: Prayer flags, pine ridges, and the world's last Vajrayana capital.

taxi.fareNote: Government sets per-km rate cards (base fare plus ~25 Nu/km) but cabs rarely run meters in practice; confirm the fare with the driver, or agree a flat rate, before departing.

emergency.medical: 112 (ambulance); 110 for fire; 1010 general emergency access line
emergency.note: Bhutan has very low crime; the Royal Bhutan Police is helpful and English-speaking in Thimphu.

avoid.reason: Stray dog packs at night and occasional late-night drunken scuffles near downtown bars are the main annoyances.

hood_desc: The walkable commercial heart of Thimphu around Norzin Lam, packed with shops, cafes, the weekend market and the National Memorial Chorten; best for first-time visitors and anyone without a car.

A quieter mid-town corridor near Tashichho Dzong and the Chubachu circle, home to international-standard hotels; suits business travelers and those wanting comfort within easy walking distance of downtown.
A pine-forested residential ridge above the city near the Motithang Takin Preserve; ideal for couples, honeymooners and travelers wanting a calmer, scenic stay a short taxi ride from downtown.
A local, laid-back southern district along the Wang Chhu river near the Buddha Dordenma statue, with traditional guesthouses; good for budget travelers and longer stays seeking an authentic feel.
A no-frills area around the inter-city bus terminal with simple hotels and guesthouses; suits backpackers and those catching early buses to Paro, Punakha or Phuentsholing.

water.note: Water is often contaminated by the time it reaches the tap; drink bottled or boiled water only.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash on boarding; city routes charge a small flat/short-hop fare in ngultrum. Most visitors instead rely on hired cars with driver or taxis given the compact, hilly center and Bhutan's guided-tourism structure.
transit.hours: Roughly 7am-9pm on main routes; no late-night service, so taxis cover evenings and early mornings.
transit.note: Bhutan has no rail or metro; the small city bus network mainly serves residents, while tourists typically travel by private/hired vehicle.

bus: Bhutan Post City Bus Service (Thimphu urban routes)
Inter-city coaches from Thimphu's Changzamtog bus terminal to Paro, Punakha, Phuentsholing and beyond

airport.name: Paro International Airport (PBH)
airport.drive: 45-60 min via the Paro-Thimphu highway (only ~46 km but winding mountain road)

tip.r: Tipping isn't traditional but is increasingly appreciated for guides, drivers, and restaurant staff in tourist-oriented spots; 5-10% or a small flat amount is plenty.

food.name: Ema Datshi
food.desc: Bhutan's national dish: whole green or dried red chillies stewed with soft local datshi cheese into a fiery sauce for red rice.

places.name: Folk Heritage Museum Restaurant
places.note: Traditional farmhouse setting serving the classic village version of ema datshi.

places.name: Babesa Village Restaurant
places.note: Set meals in bamboo bangchung inside a centuries-old house; a Thimphu institution.

places.name: Zombala Restaurant
places.note: Long-standing local favourite widely rated for its ema datshi and momo.

food.name: Kewa Datshi and Shamu Datshi
food.desc: Milder cousins of the national dish: sliced potato, or wild mushrooms, simmered with butter and melted cheese and a little chilli.

places.name: Phangu Restaurant
places.note: Home-style Bhutanese cooking with heirloom ingredients and full datshi range.

places.name: Babesa Village Restaurant
places.note: Traditional set menus include kewa datshi alongside pork and cucumber salad.

places.name: Folk Heritage Museum Restaurant
places.note: Cooks the datshi dishes over a wood stove in a restored rammed-earth house.

food.name: Momo and Hoentay
food.desc: Steamed dumplings filled with cheese, cabbage or beef, plus Haa valley hoentay, buckwheat parcels stuffed with turnip greens.

places.name: Zombala Restaurant
places.note: Best-known momo house in Thimphu, with Bhutanese and Tibetan fillings.

places.name: Folk Heritage Museum Restaurant
places.note: One of the few places serving hoentay, the buckwheat dumpling from Haa.

places.name: Ambient Cafe
places.note: Relaxed town-centre cafe popular for cheese momo and light Bhutanese plates.

food.name: Phaksha Paa (Pork with Radish and Chilli)
food.desc: Belly pork stewed with dried red chillies, radish and sometimes dried spinach; rich, smoky and eaten with red rice.

places.name: Babesa Village Restaurant
places.note: Phaksha paa and goen hogay cucumber salad anchor its traditional set meal.

places.name: Phangu Restaurant
places.note: Feels like eating in a Bhutanese home; pork dishes are a strength.

places.name: Folk Heritage Museum Restaurant
places.note: Serves the old farmhouse repertoire including dried pork and chilli stews.

food.name: Bhutanese Red Rice
food.desc: Nutty, slightly sticky red rice grown in the Paro and Thimphu valleys; the base of every Bhutanese meal, mopping up datshi sauce.

places.name: Centenary Farmers Market
places.note: Weekend market where valley farmers sell red rice, chillies and datshi cheese.

places.name: Babesa Village Restaurant
places.note: Red rice served in bangchung baskets as part of the traditional set meal.

places.name: Simply Bhutan
places.note: Living museum restaurant presenting red rice with the full traditional spread.

food.name: Jasha Maru (Spicy Minced Chicken)
food.desc: Chicken minced or chopped with tomato, ginger, garlic and green chilli into a loose, soupy stew ladled over rice.

places.name: Folk Heritage Museum Restaurant
places.note: Jasha maru is listed among its core traditional dishes.

places.name: Zombala Restaurant
places.note: Reliable local kitchen turning out chicken and beef Bhutanese stews.

places.name: Phangu Restaurant
places.note: Small, personal dining room cooking Bhutanese classics to order.

food.name: Suja (Butter Tea)
food.desc: Churned tea with yak butter and salt, poured hot and endlessly refilled; the default welcome drink in every Bhutanese home.

places.name: Folk Heritage Museum Restaurant
places.note: Butter tea served the traditional way beside the museum's restored farmhouse.

places.name: Simply Bhutan
places.note: Cultural centre where visitors are given suja and shown how it is churned.

places.name: Centenary Farmers Market
places.note: Stalls at the weekend market pour suja and sweet milk tea for shoppers.

food.name: Ara (Traditional Grain Spirit)
food.desc: Home-distilled spirit of rice, wheat or barley, sometimes served warm with butter and egg; enjoyed sparingly, as tea leads the day.

places.name: Simply Bhutan
places.note: Offers visitors a supervised taste of ara as part of its cultural tour.

places.name: Babesa Village Restaurant
places.note: Traditional house restaurant that can serve ara with the set meal on request.

places.name: The Zone
places.note: Popular Thimphu bar and grill stocking local craft beer alongside Bhutanese drinks.

landmarks: Buddha Dordenma
This colossal 51-metre gilded bronze Buddha sits atop Kuensel Phodrang hill, overlooking the Thimphu valley and glowing gold at sunset.
Tashichho Dzong
A whitewashed fortress-monastery with golden roofs housing the throne room of Bhutan's king, it dazzles visitors especially during the lively autumn Tsechu festival.
National Memorial Chorten
This large white stupa crowned with a golden spire is Thimphu's spiritual heart, where locals circumambulate and spin prayer wheels daily.
Punakha Dzong
Often visited on a day trip from Thimphu, this stunning riverside fortress at the confluence of two rivers is widely considered Bhutan's most beautiful dzong.
Simtokha Dzong
Bhutan's oldest surviving fortress, dating to 1629, features exquisite carvings and slate wall paintings that make it a favorite for architecture photography.
Changangkha Lhakhang
Perched on a ridge above the city, this 15th-century temple is one of Thimphu's oldest and offers panoramic views along with deep local devotion.
Clock Tower Square
A bustling pedestrian plaza in central Thimphu decorated with traditional Bhutanese motifs, it's a popular gathering spot for shopping, food, and people-watching.
Motithang Takin Preserve
Home to Bhutan's quirky national animal, the takin, this hillside reserve offers a fun and easy wildlife encounter just outside the capital.
Centenary Farmers Market
Thimphu's vibrant weekend market draws crowds crossing a footbridge over the Wang Chhu to browse stalls of fresh produce, cheese, and local crafts.
Thimphu Valley Viewpoints
Sweeping hillside vistas over the traditional-style buildings and forested slopes of Bhutan's uniquely low-rise, sign-free capital city.

train.note: Bhutan has no railway anywhere in the country. The nearest railheads are Hasimara and New Jalpaiguri in India; onward travel is entirely by road via the border town of Phuentsholing.

intl.op: Bhutan Post (Royal Bhutanese Government bus service)

bus.note: The cross-border Bhutan-Kolkata coach runs from Phuentsholing on the Indian border, not Thimphu - from Thimphu take a Bhutan Post bus (~6h) to Phuentsholing first. Carry your passport and Indian visa.

ferry.note: Bhutan is landlocked, so there are no ferries.
